thread.title: Intraday Update: Dow Drops 220 Points as Weird Day Gets Weirder

author: Brett Arends
title: Intraday Update: Dow Drops 220 Points as Weird Day Gets Weirder
text:
By Brett Arends April 20, 2018 1:28 p.m. ET The Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than 200 points this afternoon, pointing toward its second day in a row in the red, as Apple and rising interest rates knocked stocks for a loop. In today's Intraday Update , we...
Illustration: Bloomberg News •...explain why everyone is talking about Apple (AAPL), and not in a good way;
•...spell out why interest rates are getting worrying;
•...highlight big moves in Baker Hughes (BHGE) and Mattel (MAT);
•...follow up on Danaher (DHR) following yesterday's earnings report.
An Apple a Day Makes the Stock Market Pay It’s a weird day when General Electric (GE) is trying to lift the Dow higher and Apple (AAPL) is dragging it down.
The Cult of Cupertino tumbled nearly 4% after Mirabaud analyst Neil Campling's shock prediction that the company would axe its controversial, $1,000 flagship iPhone X this year . Campling’s prediction is very much an outlier. Most people currently disagree, and Apple (no surprise) has made no comment. But p lenty of analysts are worried about iPhone sales based on market saturation and the high price of the X.
Anything gloomy about Apple is going to drag down the whole sector.
Dow components Intel (INTC) and Microsoft (MSFT) both fell nearly 2%. As Apple fell, it helped dragged down the rest of the fashionable "Faang" (or perhaps we should now say "Aftang") complex. Tesla (TSLA) fell 2%, Amazon.com (AMZN) 1.5%, Alphabet (GOOGL) 1.2%, Facebook (FB) 0.7%, and Netflix (NFLX) 0.5%.
Illustration: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images If you want to find something else to worry about, check out long-term interest rates. The rate on the key 10-year Treasury note jumped another 0.02 percentage point to 2.94%, within a whisker of its three-year high.
Is the long, booming, eight-year era of cheap money coming to an end? The rate seems headed toward the psychological barrier of 3%. That could spark a new round of what is euphemistically called "volatility."
Meanwhile, you can’t keep up with the markets without following the president’s Twitter account. Friday morning he blasted the bull market in oil prices, blaming the OPEC cartel for keeping prices “artificially Very High” and warning this “will not be accepted!"
Big energy stocks were down: Dow components Exxon Mobil (XOM) and Chevron (CVX) both fell more than 1%. But oil traders were less impressed by the bombast. What, exactly, is the president going to do about rising oil prices? By lunchtime, crude oil futures were off just three cents at $68.30, near their highest levels in more than three years. More interesting, perhaps, was the prediction from Oman’s oil minister that oil prices would probably go no higher than $75 this year .
It wasn't all bad news. Long-term Dow laggard GE topped the leader boards, rising nearly 3% after quarterly earnings beat expectations .
S&P 500: -0.9% to 2668.67 at 1:09 p.m.
Dow 30: -218.42 points, or 0.9%, to 24,446.47
Nasdaq: -1.3% to 7147.62
Vix: +7.3% to 17.12
10-year Treasury Yield: +0.03 percentage point to 2.94%
Midday Movers Baker Hughes (BHGE) is up 2.9% to $34.70 after reporting first-quarter earnings . The oilfield-services operator earned nine cents a share, on revenue of $5.4 billion. Analysts were looking for earnings of six cents a share on revenue of $5.41 billion.
Kroger (KR) is up 1.3% to $24.49 after completing the sale of its convenience-store business and embarking on an accelerated share-repurchase plan.
Mattel (MAT) is down 5.2% to $12.74 after announcing the departure of its CEO , Margo Georgiadis, who will be replaced by Ynon Kreiz.
Stanley Black & Decker (SWK) is down 5.9% to $145.42 after reporting first-quarter earnings of $1.39 a share on revenue of $3.21 billion, ahead of the $1.35 a share and $3.1 billion revenue consensus. It also reaffirmed its full-year guidance of $8.30 to $8.50 a share, with a midpoint below the $8.44-per-share consensus.
Square (SQ) is up 2% to $1.71 after acquiring catering platform Zesty for undisclosed terms. — Teresa Rivas
Keeping an Eye on...Danaher We recommended buying Danaher (DHR) in a Feb. 3 Trader column, and while it hasn't been a great call—the stock has dropped 1.1%, including reinvested dividends, since then—that's better than the S&P 500's 2.7% loss during the same period.
At the time, I argued that "there’s something to be said for Danaher’s consistency," which was again on display when it released earnings yesterday.
Danaher reported a profit of 99 cents a share, better than the 94 cents forecast by analysts , on sales of $4.7 billion, topping estimates of $4.5 billion. Still, the stock dropped 0.9% yesterday and has followed that up with a 0.5% decline to $100.99 today. And if you look at its year-to-date chart, you have to say Danaher looks range-bound:
Still, we can deal with a range-bound stock as long as the operating trends still look good. Morgan Stanley analyst Steve Beuchaw notes that investors appear worried by the fact that Danaher didn't update its 2018 sales guidance, and that earnings-per-share guidance was lifted by just 12 cents, even after reporting a five-cent beat during the first quarter.
Still, Beuchaw walked away feeling comfortable with the company being able to hit its 4%-plus organic growth target, as well as growing margins. "We believe DHR is a stock to own in a low
growth world," he wrote.
And that will have to be good enough for now. — Ben Levisohn
